energyRt

Energy-system planning, end to end in R.

energyRt is an open-source, R-native framework and model generator for least-cost energy-system planning. Describe resources, technologies, storage, trade, and demand as reusable R objects; energyRt turns them into a capacity-expansion and dispatch model, runs the solver, and returns tidy results for analysis and reporting. Built-in validation tools can then test model structure and solution identities.

The package supplies the modeling machinery rather than a fixed dataset or scenario. It is intended for analysts, researchers, and educators who want to build transparent models at the scale and resolution their question requires without leaving the R ecosystem.

Why energyRt

  • Model the system, not the algebra. Work with energy-system components; energyRt generates sets, mappings, equations, solver files, and result tables.
  • Match resolution to the question. Define the timeframes and timeslices your model needs in a nested timescales calendar, and balance different commodities at different levels of a regional hierarchy.
  • Keep one reproducible workflow. Prepare data, compose scenarios, solve, validate, compare, plot, and report in R. Large scenarios can use Arrow-backed storage and lazy result loading.
  • Choose how and where to solve. The same model can target GLPK/MathProg, Julia/JuMP, Python/Pyomo, or GAMS, with experimental direct-matrix and remote routes for larger problems.

Time and space are yours to define

Resolution is a modelling choice, not a fixed property of the framework. The calendar below nests ANNUAL > SEASON > HOUR; the geoscale nests nation > zone > region. Both are declared by the modeller, and each commodity balances at the level its data supports.

autoplot(calendarss4h24)</code>—4seasonsx24hours,nestedunderanannualbalance.</em></td><td><em><code>plotgeoscale(topias4_h24)</code> — 4 seasons x 24 hours, nested under an annual balance.</em></td> <td><em><code>plot_geoscale(topiageoscales$continent) — regions grouped into zones, coloured by zone.

Changing a dimension does not mean rewriting the model. A model is declared once at full resolution; a coarser or sampled calendar is passed at solve time, and the geography is attached, or filtered to a sub-territory, the same way. Three arguments decide the resolution of a run:

newModel(..., calendar = calendars$s4_h24)   # declared: 4 seasons x 24 hours
solve_model(mod, name = "sampled",           # solved on a subset of its slices
            calendar = calendars$s4_h24_subset_2seasons)
setGeoscale(mod, topia$geoscales$continent)  # nation > zone > region

In a small gas-and-demand model on that calendar, sampling two of the four seasons cuts 101 timeslices to 51 and lands within 0.2% of the full solve (1759.7 against 1756.8) — the usual reason to sample while iterating and confirm at full resolution before reporting.

What’s new in v0.90

Version 0.90 is the pre-release for v1.0 and the first release since v0.50-beta, consolidating three unreleased development cycles. It brings nested time and geography into the core model, re-models storage as three priced parts, makes vintages and clusters one mechanism (including graded resources that cannot pool), reworks interpolation and scenario storage, adds structural validation and solution verification, expands analysis and reporting (levcost(), report(), draw(), autoplot()), and adopts the Apache-2.0 license.

What remains before v1.0 is testing, debugging and visualisation rather than new structure. Upgrading from 0.50 is not a drop-in — see the release notes and Upgrading first.

Quickstart

This complete model has one fuel, one power plant, and one demand. On Windows, GLPK is available with Rtools.

library(energyRt)

GAS <- newCommodity("GAS", timeframe = "ANNUAL")
ELC <- newCommodity("ELC", timeframe = "ANNUAL")

SUP_GAS <- newSupply("SUP_GAS", commodity = "GAS",
  supply = data.frame(cost = 6.0))                    # MEUR/PJ

EGAS <- newTechnology("EGAS",
  input   = list(comm = "GAS"),
  output  = list(comm = "ELC"),
  ceff    = data.frame(comm = "GAS", cinp2use = 0.55),
  invcost = list(invcost = 900),                     # MEUR/GW
  fixom   = 25,
  cap2act = 31.536,
  olife   = 25L)

DEM_ELC <- newDemand("DEM_ELC", commodity = "ELC",
  demand = data.frame(demand = 50))                  # PJ/year

mod <- newModel("HELLO",
  data = newRepository("parts", GAS, ELC, SUP_GAS, EGAS, DEM_ELC),
  region = "R1",
  discount = 0.05,
  horizon = newHorizon(
    period = 2025:2040,
    intervals = c(1, 5, 10),
    mid_is_end = TRUE
  ))

scen <- solve_model(mod, name = "BASE", solver = solver_options$glpk)

getData(scen, "vObjective", merge = TRUE)  # discounted system cost
getData(scen, "vTechCap", merge = TRUE)    # installed capacity

solve_model() interpolates and solves in one call. To inspect or modify the interpolated scenario, use the composable stages instead:

scen <- mod |>
  interpolate(name = "BASE") |>
  solve()

The Get started vignette explains the model and workflow step by step.

Core capabilities

  • Reference energy systems built from commodities, supply, demand, technologies, storage, weather, trade, taxes, subsidies, and custom constraints.
  • Capacity expansion and dispatch across multiple planning periods, with investment, retirement, operating, resource, emissions, and policy constraints.
  • Nested time using timescales. The modeler defines the calendar hierarchy, timeslices, and their duration: energyRt imposes no fixed 8,760-slice ceiling. Full-resolution, representative, and sampled calendars can all mix different balancing timeframes in one model.
  • Nested geography using geoscales, so national, zonal, and nodal balances can coexist and results can be mapped or aggregated.
  • One object, many processes. A technology declares build vintages and parallel clusters — site grades, fleet types, tranches — and expands into ordinary processes, each with its own costs, efficiency and limits. Tiered commodities and tiered weather series give a graded resource its own balance and profile per grade, so the best sites run out before the next grade starts.
  • Storage as three parts. Charger, reservoir and discharger are sized and priced separately, tied by duration and C-rate, with flows bounded by the converter rating.
  • Reusable scenarios with recorded runs, a project registry, myopic, sampled, regional and guided solve workflows, and Arrow-backed persistence for results larger than memory.
  • Checks that catch silent nonsense. Structural validation refuses a model that would solve to a meaningless answer — a flow with no capacity link, a constraint with no data behind it — and verify_solution() re-derives the model’s own identities from the results.
  • Analysis and communication through tidy getData() results, scenario and input comparison, levelized costs for technologies, storage and trade without a solver, draw() diagrams, autoplot(), maps, and HTML/PDF/Word reports for any object.
  • A path from learning to application: the packaged TOPIA teaching model develops a multi-region power system step by step, while IDEEA demonstrates a production-scale application to India’s power system.

A tour of the API

Each block below is the call shape, not a complete script — the Quickstart above is the runnable one, and every topic has an article behind it.

Processes that extend rather than multiply

A technology converts any number of inputs into any number of outputs, with auxiliary flows coupling its capacity or its flows to anything else — land per MW, water or an emission per unit of fuel. update() derives a variant instead of re-typing the object.

EGAS <- newTechnology("EGAS",
  input   = data.frame(comm = "GAS", unit = "PJ"),
  output  = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  aux     = data.frame(acomm = "CO2", unit = "kt"),
  aeff    = data.frame(acomm = "CO2", comm = "GAS", cinp2aout = 56),
  af      = data.frame(af.up = 0.85),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 900),
  cap2act = 8.76)

EGAS_CCS <- update(EGAS, name = "EGAS_CCS",
  aeff = data.frame(acomm = "CO2", comm = "GAS", cinp2aout = 5.6))

Supply, curves, trade and the model boundary

A flat price becomes a stepped supply curve in one call; corridors carry a commodity between regions, with electrical wrappers and optional loop-flow physics; imports and exports price what crosses the model boundary.

SUP_GAS  <- newSupply("SUP_GAS", commodity = "GAS",
                      supply = data.frame(ava.up = 400))
SUP_GAS  <- asSupplyCurve(SUP_GAS, price = c(4, 6, 9))   # three priced steps

AC_R1_R2 <- newACLine("AC_R1_R2", commodity = "ELC",
                      from = "R1", to = "R2", reactance = 0.1)
IMP_ELC  <- newImport("IMP_ELC", commodity = "ELC",
                      import = data.frame(price = 5000))

Variants: similar processes as one family

Build vintages and parallel clusters live on one object and expand into ordinary processes, so a fleet or a graded resource is declared once and analysed together — including its levelized cost, member by member, without a solver.

EWIN <- newTechnology("EWIN",
  output  = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  cluster = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), order = 1:3),
  capacity = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), cap.up = c(8, 16, 40)),
  invcost  = data.frame(cluster = c("01", "02", "03"), invcost = c(600, 900, 1800)),
  vintage  = data.frame(olife = 25L), cap2act = 8.76)

getVariants(mod)                      # the names before interpolating
levcost(EWIN, by_variant = TRUE)      # USD/MWh per member

Policy instruments and constraints

Taxes and subsidies levy on a commodity total or on named processes. Beyond the ~150 equation families energyRt generates from your data, newConstraint() writes an arbitrary linear restriction over declared summands — the two below are TOPIA’s own carbon-price and no-new-nuclear levers.

CT_CO2 <- newTax(name = "CT_CO2", comm = "CO2",
  tax = data.frame(year = c(2030, 2050), bal = c(0.02, 0.08)))

NO_NEW_NUC <- newConstraint(name = "NO_NEW_NUC", eq = "<=",
  for.each = data.frame(year = years, tech = "ENUC"),
  term1 = list(variable = "vTechNewCap"),
  rhs = 0, defVal = 0)

Solve strategies

The same model can be solved with perfect foresight or with any of four alternatives, each recorded as a run of the scenario.

base   <- solve_model(mod, name = "base")                    # intertemporal
myopic <- solve_myopic(mod, name = "myopic", step = 1L)      # window by window
sampled <- solve_by_sample(mod, name = "sampled")            # sampled calendars
by_reg <- solve_by_region(mod, name = "by_region")           # region by region
guided <- solve_guided(mod, name = "guided")                 # toward a target

Model size control

Resolution is the first lever — a coarser timeframe or geoframe for a commodity, a sampled calendar, a subset of regions. Folding and sparse storage are the second: they drop what does not vary and what equals a default, losslessly.

scen <- interpolate_model(mod, fold = TRUE, sparse = TRUE)
model_size(scen)              # rows per parameter, largest first
scen <- trim_parameters(scen) # drop rows no mapping indexes

Scenarios, tracking and queries

A project registry keyed on path records every model, scenario and dataset, so a study with thousands of runs stays addressable by name. Content hashes say whether two things are really the same, and results are queried and compared without leaving R.

reg  <- load_registry()
scen <- getScenario("base")                     # by name, from the registry
scenario_runs(scen)                             # every solve of this scenario
model_hash(mod); object_hash(EGAS)              # content, not file names

getData(scen, name = "vTechCap", merge = TRUE, variants = TRUE)
compare_scenarios(list(base = base, carbon_tax = tax_run))

Visualisation and auto-reporting 

draw(EGAS)                                            # the process diagram
autoplot(scen, type = "generation", comm = "ELC", by = "cluster")
plot_map(scen, name = "vTechNewCap")                  # any variable with a region
report(scen, template = "full", format = "html")      # a full scenario datasheet

One model, many representations and solve routes

The model definition is independent of the mathematical-programming runtime. Choose a representation and solve route without rewriting the energy-system model.

Route What it does Good fit
GLPK / MathProg Writes MathProg and solves with GLPK First models, teaching, and transparent local runs
Julia / JuMP Writes JuMP for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, CPLEX, or cuOpt Larger local models and a choice of algorithms
Python / Pyomo Writes Pyomo for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, or CPLEX Python-based solver environments
GAMS Writes GAMS for solvers such as CPLEX or CBC Existing institutional GAMS workflows
multimod (experimental) Converts through a common AST to LaTeX, backend code, or an LP/MPS matrix Translation, mathematical documentation, inspection, and direct LP assembly

multimod is more than another solver backend. It parses energyRt’s model into a language-neutral abstract syntax tree, from which it can render the mathematical formulation in LaTeX, emit code for other modeling languages, or skip generated model code and assemble the LP matrix directly. The direct route writes MPS and avoids the symbolic model-build step that can dominate time and memory on large linear problems.

The same separation extends to remote execution. NEOS can run supported solver jobs remotely. The experimental mmcloud route sends model files to cloud hardware, runs the solver there, streams its progress, and retrieves the solution. Together, multimod and mmcloud let energyRt assemble a large LP locally and solve it on cloud GPUs when it exceeds the practical capacity of a workstation.

See Solver backends for setup, presets, limitations, and validation guidance.

Installation

Install the development release from GitHub:

pak::pkg_install("optimal2050/energyRt")

pak installs energyRt’s R dependencies, including the optimal2050 packages listed in DESCRIPTION. You also need at least one solver runtime. On Windows, Rtools includes GLPK; on other platforms, install GLPK separately or configure Julia/JuMP, Python/Pyomo, or GAMS.

After installation, check the local setup:

library(energyRt)
en_setup()
en_check_dependencies()

See the installation guide for platform-specific instructions.

Upgrading from earlier versions

v0.90 removes deprecated names and compatibility shims from the 0.8 series and changes several serialized model and scenario structures. Rebuild saved inputs from their source definitions and review the release notes before comparing results.

To reproduce a pre-2026 project without migrating it, install the frozen legacy release:

pak::pkg_install("optimal2050/energyRt@v0.50-beta")

energyRt v0.90 is under active development. Please report bugs and proposed improvements in the issue tracker. The package website is https://energyrt.org.
